title: Trigonometry
description: Questions on radians, sine and cosine, right triangles, identities, graphs, the tangent, turns and triangles.

questions.question: How many radians make a full turn?
questions.explanation: A full turn travels once round a circle of radius $$1$$, which has length $$2\pi$$ (:ref{#radian-arc-sector}). Half a turn is $$\pi$$.

questions.question: What is $$135^\circ$$ in radians?
questions.explanation: Multiply by $$\frac{\pi}{180}$$ (:ref{#radian}): $$\frac{135\pi}{180} = \frac{3\pi}{4}$$. As a check, $$135^\circ$$ is three quarters of a straight angle, and a straight angle is $$\pi$$.

questions.question: What is special about an angle of $$1$$ radian at the centre of a circle?
options: It cuts an arc of length $$1$$ whatever the radius
It cuts off a sector of area $$1$$ whatever the radius
It cuts an arc as long as the radius
questions.explanation: An angle of $$x$$ radians cuts an arc of length $$rx$$ (:ref{#radian-arc-sector}), so with $$x = 1$$ the arc is $$r$$, as long as the radius. That is about $$57.3^\circ$$.

questions.question: What is the area of the sector cut by an angle of $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$ from a disc of radius $$4$$?
questions.explanation: The sector has area $$\frac12 r^2 x$$ (:ref{#radian-arc-sector}): $$\frac12 \cdot 16 \cdot \frac{\pi}{4} = 2\pi$$. It is an eighth of the disc, whose area is $$16\pi$$.

questions.question: Which turn is the same as $$G_{7\pi/2}$$?
questions.explanation: $$\frac{7\pi}{2} = \frac{3\pi}{2} + 2\pi$$, and a whole turn more makes no difference (:ref{#radian-turns}).

questions.question: Turn the point $$(1, 0)$$ about the origin by $$x$$ radians. Where does it land?
questions.explanation: That is the definition (:ref{#sine-cosine}): cosine is how far across, and sine is how far up.

questions.question: Which equation holds for every number $$x$$?
questions.explanation: The point $$(\cos x, \sin x)$$ lies on the unit circle, at distance $$1$$ from $$O$$ (:ref{#pythagorean-identity}). The sum $$\cos x + \sin x$$ is $$\sqrt2$$ at $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$, so it isn't always $$1$$.

questions.question: For $$x = 2.5$$, which is between $$\frac{\pi}{2}$$ and $$\pi$$, what are the signs of $$\cos x$$ and $$\sin x$$?
questions.explanation: The point is in the second quadrant, left of the $$y$$-axis and above the $$x$$-axis (:ref{#quadrant-signs}). In fact $$\cos 2.5 \approx -0.80$$ and $$\sin 2.5 \approx 0.60$$.

questions.question: If $$\sin x = \frac35$$ and the point for $$x$$ is in the second quadrant, what is $$\cos x$$?
questions.explanation: $$\cos^2 x = 1 - \frac{9}{25} = \frac{16}{25}$$ (:ref{#pythagorean-identity}), so $$\cos x = \pm\frac45$$, and cosine is negative in the second quadrant (:ref{#quadrant-signs}).

questions.question: A calculator in radian mode gives $$\sin 30 \approx -0.988$$. Why isn't it $$\frac12$$?
options: Sine is negative for big angles
questions.explanation: In radian mode, $$30$$ means $$30$$ radians, almost five full turns. Switch to degree mode, or type $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$, to get $$\frac12$$ (:ref{#radian}).

questions.question: What is $$\sin\frac{\pi}{6}$$, the sine of $$30^\circ$$?
questions.explanation: Half an equilateral triangle with sides $$2$$ has a side $$1$$ opposite its $$30^\circ$$ angle and hypotenuse $$2$$ (:ref{#sin-cos-30-60}).

questions.question: What is $$\cos\frac{\pi}{4}$$, the cosine of $$45^\circ$$?
questions.explanation: Half a square with sides $$1$$ has a diagonal $$\sqrt2$$, so the cosine is $$\frac{1}{\sqrt2} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}$$ (:ref{#sin-cos-45}).

questions.question: Sine at $$0, \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}$$ follows the pattern $$\frac{\sqrt0}{2}, \frac{\sqrt1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \frac{\sqrt4}{2}$$. What does cosine do at the same angles?
questions.explanation: Cosine at an angle is sine at the angle that makes a right angle with it (:ref{#complement-identities}), so the list runs the other way. The triangles are the reason the values are right (:ref{#sin-cos-30-60}).

questions.question: A seat on a wheel of radius $$10$$ m starts level with the centre and turns by $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$. How far above the centre is it?
questions.explanation: It is at $$(10\cos\frac{\pi}{6}, 10\sin\frac{\pi}{6})$$ (:ref{#circle-point-radius}), so its height is $$10 \cdot \frac12 = 5$$ m.

questions.topic: Sine and cosine in right triangles
questions.question: In a right triangle, what is $$\sin\theta$$ for one of the other angles $$\theta$$?
options: Opposite side divided by adjacent side
questions.explanation: Put the corner at $$O$$ with the adjacent side along the $$x$$-axis, and the far corner is the hypotenuse times $$(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$$ (:ref{#right-triangle-ratios}).

questions.topic: Sine and cosine in right triangles
questions.question: Two right triangles have the same angle $$\theta$$, but one is three times as big. How do their values of $$\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$$ compare?
options: The big one's is three times as big
The big one's is nine times as big
The big one's is a third
questions.explanation: Both ratios equal $$\sin\theta$$ (:ref{#right-triangle-ratios}). Zooming multiplies both sides by the same number, which cancels.

questions.topic: Sine and cosine in right triangles
questions.question: A $$4$$ m ladder leans against a wall, making $$\frac{\pi}{3}$$ ($$60^\circ$$) with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
questions.explanation: The height is the side opposite the angle, so it is $$4\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = 4 \cdot \frac{\sqrt3}{2}$$ (:ref{#right-triangle-ratios}).

questions.topic: Sine and cosine in right triangles
questions.question: What does $$\sin^{-1}\frac12$$ mean?
options: The angle in $$[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}]$$ whose sine is $$\frac12$$, which is $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$
questions.explanation: The $$-1$$ means the inverse, not a power (:ref{#inverse-sin-cos}). The button finds the angle.

questions.topic: Sine and cosine in right triangles
questions.question: How many numbers $$x$$ with $$0 \le x < 2\pi$$ have $$\sin x = \frac12$$?
questions.explanation: Two points of the unit circle are at height $$\frac12$$, mirror images in the $$y$$-axis (:ref{#same-sine}). The button gives only the one on the right.

questions.topic: Sine and cosine in right triangles
questions.question: What is the side of the regular hexagon in a circle of radius $$3$$?
questions.explanation: The side is $$2r\sin\frac{\pi}{n} = 6\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = 3$$ (:ref{#polygon-side}), as long as the radius.

questions.question: Which pair is right for every number $$x$$?
questions.explanation: Turning by $$-x$$ lands on the mirror image in the $$x$$-axis: the same distance across, the opposite height (:ref{#negative-angle}).

questions.question: The point for $$\pi - x$$ is the point for $$x$$ moved by which move?
options: The flip in the line $$y = x$$
questions.explanation: The flip in the $$y$$-axis keeps the height and changes the sign across, so $$\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$$ and $$\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x$$ (:ref{#supplement-identities}).

questions.question: What is $$\sin(x + \frac{\pi}{2})$$?
questions.explanation: A quarter turn sends $$(a, b)$$ to $$(-b, a)$$, so the new height is the old distance across (:ref{#quarter-turn-identities}).

questions.question: What is $$\cos\frac{4\pi}{3}$$?
questions.explanation: $$\frac{4\pi}{3} = \pi + \frac{\pi}{3}$$, in the third quadrant with reference angle $$\frac{\pi}{3}$$, where cosine is negative (:ref{#symmetries-reference-values}). So it is $$-\cos\frac{\pi}{3}$$.

questions.question: What is $$\cos\frac{7\pi}{4}$$?
questions.explanation: $$\frac{7\pi}{4}$$ is in the fourth quadrant with reference angle $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$, and cosine is positive there (:ref{#symmetries-reference-values}).

questions.topic: The graphs of sine and cosine
questions.question: How often does the graph of $$y = \sin x$$ repeat?
questions.explanation: A whole turn brings the point back where it started (:ref{#periodic}), and no shorter shift works (:ref{#graphs-least-period}).

questions.topic: The graphs of sine and cosine
questions.question: How is the graph of cosine related to the graph of sine?
options: It is the sine graph flipped upside down
It is the sine graph stretched
It is the sine graph slid left by $$\frac{\pi}{2}$$
questions.explanation: $$\cos x = \sin(x + \frac{\pi}{2})$$ (:ref{#cosine-shift}), so the cosine reaches each height $$\frac{\pi}{2}$$ earlier.

questions.topic: The graphs of sine and cosine
questions.question: What is the smallest period of $$y = \sin 3x$$?
questions.explanation: For $$b > 0$$, $$\sin bx$$ has smallest period $$\frac{2\pi}{b}$$ (:ref{#squeezed-period}): three waves fit where sine has one.

questions.topic: The graphs of sine and cosine
questions.question: For which numbers $$x$$ is $$\cos x = 0$$?
questions.explanation: The points of the unit circle with first coordinate $$0$$ are $$E_2$$ and $$-E_2$$, at $$\frac{\pi}{2}$$ and $$\frac{3\pi}{2}$$, half a turn apart (:ref{#trig-zeros}).

questions.topic: The graphs of sine and cosine
questions.question: How high does the graph of $$y = 3\sin x$$ reach?
questions.explanation: Every height of the sine graph is multiplied by $$3$$, and sine reaches $$1$$ at most (:ref{#sine-and-cosine-bounds}).

questions.question: What is $$\tan x$$?
questions.explanation: That is the definition (:ref{#tangent}). It is the slope of the ray at angle $$x$$ (:ref{#tangent-slope}).

questions.question: What is $$\tan\frac{\pi}{3}$$?
questions.explanation: $$\frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{\cos(\pi/3)} = \frac{\sqrt3/2}{1/2} = \sqrt3$$ (:ref{#tangent}, :ref{#sin-cos-30-60}).

questions.question: From $$20$$ m away, the top of a tree is $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$ above level. How tall is the tree above eye level?
questions.explanation: The height is the opposite side and $$20$$ m is the adjacent side, so the height is $$20\tan\frac{\pi}{4} = 20$$ (:ref{#tangent-slope}).

questions.question: A road climbs with a gradient of $$10\%$$: it rises $$1$$ m for every $$10$$ m across. About what angle does it make with level ground?
questions.explanation: The angle has tangent $$0.1$$, so it is $$\tan^{-1} 0.1 \approx 5.7^\circ$$ (:ref{#inverse-tan}).

questions.question: If $$\tan x = \frac34$$, what is $$\sec^2 x$$?
questions.explanation: $$1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x$$ (:ref{#tan-sec-identity}), so $$\sec^2 x = 1 + \frac{9}{16}$$.

questions.question: How often does the tangent repeat?
questions.explanation: A half turn changes the sign of both sine and cosine, so their ratio stays the same (:ref{#tangent-period}).

questions.question: Which is true for every $$a$$ and $$b$$?
questions.explanation: That is the addition formula (:ref{#addition-formulas}). With $$a = b = \frac{\pi}{4}$$, $$\sin a + \sin b = \sqrt2$$, more than $$1$$, so sines don't add.

questions.question: The proof of $$\cos(a - b) = \cos a\cos b + \sin a\sin b$$ works out one distance in two ways. Which distance?
options: Between the points for $$a$$ and $$b$$ on the unit circle
From the origin to the point for $$a$$
From the point for $$a$$ to the $$x$$-axis
Between $$a$$ and $$b$$ on the number line
questions.explanation: The chord between the points for $$a$$ and $$b$$, turned back by $$b$$, becomes the chord from $$(1, 0)$$ to the point for $$a - b$$. Turns keep distances (:ref{#cos-difference}).

questions.question: What is $$\cos\frac{\pi}{12}$$, the cosine of $$15^\circ$$?
questions.explanation: $$\frac{\pi}{12} = \frac{\pi}{3} - \frac{\pi}{4}$$, so it is $$\cos\frac{\pi}{3}\cos\frac{\pi}{4} + \sin\frac{\pi}{3}\sin\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt2 + \sqrt6}{4}$$ (:ref{#addition-formulas}).

questions.question: If $$\sin x = 0.6$$ and $$0 < x < \frac{\pi}{2}$$, what is $$\sin 2x$$?
questions.explanation: $$\cos x = 0.8$$, and $$\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x = 2(0.6)(0.8)$$ (:ref{#double-angle}). Doubling the sine would give $$1.2$$, more than any sine can be.

questions.question: Which formula gives $$\cos^2 x$$ from the cosine of $$2x$$?
questions.explanation: $$\cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x - 1$$ (:ref{#double-angle}); solve for $$\cos^2 x$$ (:ref{#half-angle}). Check with $$x = 0$$: both sides are $$1$$.

questions.question: What makes an equation in $$x$$ an identity?
options: It holds for every $$x$$ where both sides are defined
It holds for at least one $$x$$
It has a sine in it
questions.explanation: That is the definition (:ref{#identity}). An equation that holds for only some $$x$$ is one to solve.

questions.question: You put $$x = 1$$ into both sides of an equation and get the same number. What does that show?
options: Nothing for certain: it is evidence, not a proof
questions.explanation: One matching value can be a coincidence. A value that doesn't match shows the equation is not an identity; a proof is needed to show it is one (:ref{#identity}).

questions.question: Which value of $$x$$ shows that $$\sin 2x = 2\sin x$$ is not an identity?
options: $$x = \frac{\pi}{2}$$: the left is $$0$$ and the right is $$2$$
No value: it is an identity
questions.explanation: $$\sin\pi = 0$$ but $$2\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 2$$. At $$x = 0$$ and $$x = \pi$$ both sides are $$0$$, which is why one check is never enough. The right formula is $$\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$$ (:ref{#double-angle}).

questions.question: Which describes every solution of $$\sin x = \frac12$$?
questions.explanation: The two points at height $$\frac12$$ are at $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$ and $$\pi - \frac{\pi}{6}$$, and each repeats every whole turn (:ref{#sine-solutions}).

questions.question: Solving $$\sin 2x = \sin x$$, why not divide both sides by $$\sin x$$?
options: It loses the solutions where $$\sin x = 0$$
It is against the rules to divide by a sine
It gives the wrong answer for every $$x$$
questions.explanation: Write $$2\sin x\cos x - \sin x = \sin x(2\cos x - 1) = 0$$ instead (:ref{#double-angle}). Then $$\sin x = 0$$ or $$\cos x = \frac12$$, and dividing would have thrown the first away.

questions.question: What are polar coordinates for the point $$(-2, 2)$$, with the angle in $$[0, 2\pi)$$?
questions.explanation: The distance is $$\sqrt{4 + 4}$$, and the point is in the second quadrant on the line $$y = -x$$, at $$\frac{3\pi}{4}$$ (:ref{#polar-coordinates}).

questions.question: For the point $$(-1, -1)$$, $$\tan^{-1}\frac{y}{x} = \tan^{-1} 1 = \frac{\pi}{4}$$. Is $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$ an angle for the point?
options: No: the point is in the third quadrant, so add $$\pi$$ to get $$\frac{5\pi}{4}$$
questions.explanation: $$(1, 1)$$ and $$(-1, -1)$$ give the same ratio $$\frac{y}{x}$$. When $$x < 0$$, add $$\pi$$ (:ref{#rotations-polar-angle}).

questions.question: What does the turn by $$\frac{\pi}{3}$$ about $$O$$ do to $$(4, 0)$$?
questions.explanation: By :ref{#rotation-formula}, $$(4, 0)$$ goes to $$(4\cos\frac{\pi}{3}, 4\sin\frac{\pi}{3}) = (2, 2\sqrt3)$$.

questions.question: What does the formula $$(x\cos\varphi - y\sin\varphi,\ x\sin\varphi + y\cos\varphi)$$ give for $$\varphi = \frac{\pi}{2}$$?
questions.explanation: $$\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0$$ and $$\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1$$, so the formula becomes $$(-y, x)$$, the quarter turn of earlier chapters (:ref{#rotation-formula}).

questions.question: What is the product $$M_\alpha M_\beta$$ of the matrices of two turns?
questions.explanation: Turning by $$\beta$$ and then by $$\alpha$$ is turning by $$\alpha + \beta$$, and multiplying out the matrices gives the addition formulas (:ref{#rotation-composite}).

questions.question: What is the angle between the steps $$(3, 1)$$ and $$(1, 2)$$?
questions.explanation: The dot product is $$5$$ and the lengths are $$\sqrt{10}$$ and $$\sqrt5$$, so the cosine is $$\frac{5}{\sqrt{50}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$$ (:ref{#dot-angle}).

questions.question: Two sides of a triangle are $$5$$ and $$8$$ with $$\frac{\pi}{3}$$ between them. What is the third side?
questions.explanation: $$c^2 = 25 + 64 - 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 8 \cdot \frac12 = 49$$ (:ref{#law-of-cosines}). $$\sqrt{89}$$ is what Pythagoras would give with a right angle.

questions.question: What does the law of cosines become when the angle $$\gamma$$ is a right angle?
questions.explanation: $$\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0$$, so $$c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos\gamma$$ becomes $$c^2 = a^2 + b^2$$ (:ref{#law-of-cosines}).

questions.question: A triangle has sides $$6$$ and $$4$$ with $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$ between them. What is its area?
questions.explanation: The area is $$\frac12 ab\sin\gamma = \frac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 4 \cdot \frac12$$ (:ref{#area-sine}).

questions.question: Why does a zoom keep every angle?
options: Steps are multiplied by $$r$$, so the dot product over the lengths, the cosine, is unchanged
questions.explanation: The dot product is multiplied by $$r^2$$ and each length by $$r$$, so the cosine is the same, and an angle between $$0$$ and $$\pi$$ is fixed by its cosine (:ref{#zoom-angles}). This proves the last zoom rule.
